title: The monkey and the crocodile
hook: caught mid-river, the monkey says he left his heart up in the fig tree (Jataka 208)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the quarrelling quails, who lifted the net together until they started bickering. Your line was together we lift the net. What did you lift without keeping score? Day eighty-nine.

Sometimes the trouble only shows itself halfway across. The friendly stranger isn't friendly. The deal isn't a deal. And there's no way out except quick thinking. On the bank of the Ganges, the story goes, there lived a monkey, strong and clever. Tradition says it was the Buddha, in an earlier life. In the river lived a crocodile, and the crocodile's wife had been watching the monkey leap through the trees. And one day she said to her husband: I have a craving. I want to eat that monkey's heart.
screen: `HALFWAY ACROSS.` → `A MONKEY ON THE GANGES.` → `I WANT THAT MONKEY'S HEART.`

segments.voice: The crocodile swims up to the bank and calls to the monkey, all friendliness. Why do you stay on this side, eating the same old fruit? Across the river there are mango trees, jackfruit, the sweetest fruit you've ever tasted. Climb on my back, and I'll take you. The monkey thinks that sounds wonderful, and hops on. And the crocodile swims out into the middle of the river. Then he starts to sink. Water up to the monkey's knees. His chest. Hey, the monkey says, what are you doing? And the crocodile, sure he's won, tells him the truth. I'm not taking you anywhere. My wife wants your heart, and I'm going to drown you and bring it to her. Now the monkey could panic. He's in deep water with a crocodile underneath him. He can't fight. He can't swim to shore. Instead he laughs. Oh, friend, you should have said so! We monkeys don't keep our hearts inside us when we're out and about. We'd smash them to pieces, jumping from branch to branch. We hang them up in a tree for safekeeping. See that fig tree over there, with all the round fruit hanging on it? Those are our hearts. Take me back and I'll give you mine. And the crocodile, not the brightest, turns around and swims to the bank. The monkey leaps off his back, up into the fig tree, and calls down: you big fool. Did you really think anyone keeps his heart in a treetop? You're huge, but you have no wits at all. What makes this one lovely is where the monkey's strength came from. Not muscles. Not claws. A calm mind, in deep water. He stayed clear, and saw a way out that force could never find.
screen: `THE SWEETEST FRUIT ACROSS THE RIVER.` · `THE CROCODILE STARTS TO SINK.` · `MY HEART IS IN THE FIG TREE.` · `A CALM MIND IN DEEP WATER.` · then, large: `KEEP YOUR WITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use wit instead of force once, starting with a calm mind. Settle and breathe. Think of a situation where you usually push. An argument. A negotiation. A kid who won't put their shoes on. Picture yourself in the middle of the river with it. Instead of struggling, take one slow breath, and ask: what's another way out? A joke? A question? A different door? Let an idea come. The bell holds the time.
The monkey and the crocodile. Tricked into deep water, the monkey stayed calm, said his heart was in the fig tree, and got away.
screen: `THE MONKEY AND THE CROCODILE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep your wits. Today, when something goes wrong fast, take one breath before you react, and look for the clever way out. Day eighty-nine.

howItsDone: The monkey and the crocodile is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, appears in early Buddhist carving, and is found in the Panchatantra as well.

fork.setup: you're a monkey in the middle of a river, on a crocodile's back. he's sinking, and says he wants your heart. what do you do?
options: jump off and try to swim.
tell him your heart is back in the fig tree.
beg him to let you go.
fork.reveal: the monkey laughs and says monkeys keep their hearts in trees. the crocodile swims back, and the monkey leaps to safety.

original.note: Pali: crocodile. The story is the Sumsumara Jataka.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly animal story with a trick at the end.
what it means: a lesson in keeping a clear mind in danger: wit instead of force.
what a scholar hears: Sumsumara Jataka, no. 208, with a close variant in the Vanarinda Jataka (no. 57); a version frames book 4 of the Panchatantra; carved at Bharhut.

notes: Retold in paraphrase from Jataka 208; the fruit named (mangoes, jackfruit) and the monkey's closing taunt are summarized. Confirm details.
